newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS - Analysts welcome Hungary OTP, Matav moves.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Analysts welcome Hungary OTP, Matav moves.

text.p: Hungarian plans to reduce the compulsory state stake in telecom company Matav and OTP Bank to one golden share will stimulate the markets but still leave room for government intervention, analysts say.

"It's great news for the market in general because OTP and Matav are very good quality companies," Gabor Sitanyi of ING Barings in London told Reuters. "There are lots of new investors out there who would like to have exposure to them."
The Hungarian government said last week it planned to amend the privatisation law's regulations on what stakes the state should maintain permanently in some 80 companies.
Included are Matav and OTP, in which the current minimum state stake of 25 percent plus one share would be replaced by a golden share with certain veto rights.

Tommy Erdei of ABN AMRO Hoare Govett warned that in the case of Matav, which is 67 percent owned by a 50-50 consortium of Deutsche Telekom and Ameritech Corp, the replacement of the state's 25 percent with a golden share will not always mean a reduction in state influence.

"With a 25 percent stake, if the other 75 percent can agree then they can do what they want even over the government's objections, whereas with the golden share in certain cases they just won't be able to," he said.
Erdei cited the hypothetical example of a management decision to close an unprofitable unit.

"The government is not looking at these decisions the way other investors are as to how much it improves the company's finances. It has this other area where it wants to protect its interests -- that is public opinion."

Another problem is the sheer size of the state's 25 percent stake in Matav, an offering of which would have to be combined with an already planned sale of around 16 percent Deutsche Telekom/Ameritech shares.
"It will be difficult to harmonise the whole thing because that 25 and 16 percent could give you $1.4 billion so it has to be played carefully," said Sitanyi.

With such a large issue both Sitanyi and Erdei believe the state privatisation agency APV will follow the example of oil company MOL and pharmaceutical company Richter by releasing the shares in tranches.
However, the equation is complicated by upcoming elections due around May next year, says Sitanyi.
"(The offering) really has to be this year as the markets don't receive January issues very well and to postpone it until later on you're going to bump into the problem of a new government.
"Two months before and after the elections APV is not in a position to make serious decisions as there are officials coming and going."

Analysts believe the case of OTP is more straightforward, both because the total value of the reduced government minimum stake is smaller at $150 million and because in the absence of other large shareholders, the government has a freer hand.
Sitanyi believes OTP's retail network -- still almost a monopoly in many parts of Hungary -- could make it attractive to U.S investors.

"It could be popular in the U.S. because of the size of the bank...and OTP could make the case that although competition is intensifying in the banking industry, in the retail segment, at least, competition for the moment is less intense."
Hungary's current macroeconomic trends of falling inflation and rising GDP growth also make the banking sector attractive, he said.
On the Budapest Stock Exchange OTP closed on Monday up 40 at 4,580.
